title: A Pill Just Doubled Survival for Pancreatic Cancer. The KRAS Mutation It Targets Hits South Asians Hard.
excerpt: Daraxonrasib cracked the 'undruggable' gene behind 90 per cent of pancreatic cancers. The FDA is fast-tracking it. Here is why South Asians should care.
body:
Oncologists at the American Society of Clinical Oncology's annual meeting rarely stand up mid-presentation. Last week, thousands of them did. The data on the screen showed something the field had chased for decades: a pill that doubled how long patients with advanced pancreatic cancer survived.

The drug is daraxonrasib, developed by Revolution Medicines. In a Phase 3 trial of nearly 500 patients whose cancer had already beaten chemotherapy, those given standard second-line chemo lived an average of 6.7 months. Patients who received daraxonrasib instead lived more than 13 months — a hazard ratio of 0.40, meaning the drug cut the risk of death by 60 per cent.

Tumours shrank in three times as many patients. Quality of life improved. Pain decreased. The standing ovation was not performative. It was recognition that a wall had finally been cracked.

## The 'Undruggable' Gene That Drives 90 Per Cent of Pancreatic Cancers

Pancreatic cancer has long been among the deadliest malignancies, largely because its primary driver — a mutated gene called KRAS — was considered impossible to target with medication. When KRAS mutates, it gets stuck in the "on" position, forcing cancer cells to grow uncontrollably. More than 90 per cent of pancreatic cancers carry this mutation.

Daraxonrasib works by directly blocking the mutant KRAS protein, something researchers tried and failed to do for over 30 years. The drug's side effects — mostly mouth sores and skin rashes — are significantly less severe than chemotherapy, though some patients describe them as intense. Former US Senator Ben Sasse, who participated in the trial, called the experience "nuclear" but said the alternative was worse.

The results are already being built upon. On Monday, Tango Therapeutics announced that combining its drug vopimetostat with daraxonrasib shrank tumours in 11 of 12 patients — a 92 per cent response rate. Ninety per cent of patients survived without disease progression for six months. Tango's stock jumped 45 per cent on the news.

## Why South Asians Cannot Afford to Ignore This

The South Asian diaspora's relationship with pancreatic cancer runs through its most prevalent chronic disease: type 2 diabetes. Multiple large-scale studies have established that long-standing diabetes roughly doubles the risk of developing pancreatic cancer. South Asians develop diabetes earlier, at lower body weights, and at higher rates than almost any other ethnic group. In the US, Indian Americans have a diabetes prevalence of 12.6 per cent compared to 7.5 per cent for white Americans.

The connection is not abstract. Chronic hyperinsulinaemia — the sustained high insulin levels that characterise South Asian metabolic dysfunction — creates an environment that promotes pancreatic cell proliferation. The same metabolic pathways that make South Asians more susceptible to diabetes may make them more vulnerable to the cancers it enables.

Pancreatic cancer is also notoriously difficult to detect early. By the time symptoms appear — unexplained weight loss, jaundice, back pain — the disease is usually advanced. For a community where regular screening beyond basic bloodwork is uncommon, this is a compounding risk.

## What Happens Next

The FDA has fast-tracked daraxonrasib for approval. If granted, the drug could be available in clinics within months. Researchers are already testing whether it can fight other KRAS-driven cancers, including lung, colon, ovarian, and endometrial cancers — a pipeline that could eventually benefit millions of patients worldwide.

For the diaspora, the immediate takeaway is not the drug itself but the reminder underneath it. Pancreatic cancer thrives in the metabolic conditions that South Asians disproportionately carry. Managing blood sugar, reducing visceral fat, and pushing for screening conversations with physicians are not generic health advice — they are risk-specific interventions for a community that diabetes hits harder and earlier than most.

The wall around pancreatic cancer has been breached. The question for South Asians is whether the conditions that build behind it are being addressed before the diagnosis arrives.
